interface.name: lxb_shell_v1

description.summary: private channel between LineXinBar and its session shell

interface.description:
Layer-shell lets a shell draw itself, but says nothing about the two things a console-style session needs: a hardware button that reaches the shell even while a fullscreen application owns the keyboard, and a way for the shell to end that application or the session.
This interface supplies exactly those. It is a privileged protocol: the compositor offers it only to the programs its own session is made of — the session shell it started, and the desktop portal that draws its questions through the shell — and refuses it to every other client.
That is deliberately narrower than wlr-layer-shell's footing, which this interface used to claim. A LineXinBar session runs a great deal that the user did not write and the compositor cannot vet: Valve's client and every game it starts, whatever the software hub installed, a browser. The requests here hide any application from the screen while leaving it running, close anybody's window, inject key and pointer events, and end the session — none of which is a thing an ordinary client of a session should be able to do to the rest of it.
The compositor decides from the credentials the kernel puts on the connection, never from anything a client says about itself. A client that may not bind it is not shown the global at all, and an attempt to bind it regardless is a protocol error.
The two programs it does offer it to do not get the same interface. The session shell may use all of it. The desktop portal — which exists to put questions from applications outside the session to the user — may use offer_kind, ask_to_pick_files and ask_to_share, and receives the answers to those; every other request is a not_permitted error on its object.

enum.name: error

description.summary: what a client got wrong

enum.description: Sent as a fatal protocol error on the object it happened to.

entry.name: not_permitted
entry.summary: this request is not one this client may make

request.name: destroy

description.summary: stop receiving session events

request.description: Releases the object. Any other bound instance keeps receiving events.

request.name: close_foreground

description.summary: ask the foreground application to close

request.description:
Requests that the compositor close the topmost application window, the one named by the most recent foreground event.
The request is polite: the application is asked to close and may refuse or prompt the user, exactly as if its own close button had been used. It is silently ignored when no application window exists.
Superseded by close_output_foreground for shells that draw on more than one display.

request.name: close_output_foreground

description.summary: ask the application on one display to close

request.description:
As close_foreground, but scoped to a display: the topmost application window on that display is asked to close.
A shell whose overlay belongs to one display has to be able to say so. Otherwise the entry it drew as "Close Celeste" closes whatever happens to be topmost across the session instead.
Silently ignored when that display has no application window, or when the output is gone.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to act on

request.name: quit

description.summary: end the session

request.description: Shuts the compositor down. On a native session this logs the user out.

request.name: set_launch_output

description.summary: choose the display new applications open on

request.description:
Names the display the user is currently driving, so that an application started by the shell opens there.
Without this the compositor can only infer the answer from keyboard focus, which is wrong in exactly the case that matters: a shell drawn over a running application gives focus back to that application before the newly started one maps, so the new window would join the old one's display instead of the one it was picked on. A shell showing one surface per display already knows which display that is.
The choice persists until it is changed. It is a preference, not a constraint: the compositor still places windows itself, and falls back to its own policy when the named output is gone.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: display to open applications on

request.name: set_driven_output

description.summary: which display the user is at

request.description:
Names the display the user is driving, for every question that is about where the person is rather than about where a window belongs: which display's topmost window gets the keyboard back when something closes, which display's game is the X screen's active window, and which display a screenshot binding photographs.
It is not set_launch_output, and the two came apart because they had been one field answering both. A shell holds the launch answer on the display a game was started from for as long as that game is on its way, which is right — an application belongs to the screen it was launched from, however far the user wanders while it loads. Read as "where the user is", that same held value walks the keyboard and _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW off to a screen nobody is looking at, for as long as a game takes to open. So the shell says both, and says them separately.
The choice persists until it is changed, and it is a preference rather than a constraint: the compositor falls back to its own reading — the display holding keyboard focus, then the one under the pointer — when the named output is gone or was never named.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display being driven

request.name: place_launch

description.summary: where one launch's window belongs

request.description:
Files one launch under the display it was started from, so that the window it turns into opens there whatever else has been started since.
set_launch_output is one value for the session, and a session can be loading two things on two displays at once. Whichever launch that one value happens to name is where *every* window that maps goes — so two games started on two screens, whose windows arrive in the other order, open on each other's displays. This is the same answer per launch: the compositor keeps a record for each and places a window it can match against the record's own output, and falls back to set_launch_output for a window it cannot match.
The record is matched two ways, and either is enough. pid is the process the shell started, and a window is that launch's if the process behind it is that pid or anything descended from it — a wrapper script, a launcher, a game re-executed under a runtime. app_id is what the window will call itself where the shell knows it and there is no process to name: a game handed to a store client is started by the client rather than by the shell, and arrives under a class the shell can predict. Pass 0 for pid or an empty app_id where the shell has neither, which files a record that only its output is read from.
launch is the shell's own number for this press. It means nothing to the compositor beyond telling one record from another, and a number used again replaces the record it named. A record is dropped by forget_launch, by the display it names going away, and when nothing has matched it for long enough that no window is coming.

arg.name: launch
arg.summary: the shell's own number for this press

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display it was started from

arg.name: pid
arg.summary: the process started, or 0 for none

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: what its window will call itself, or empty

request.name: forget_launch

description.summary: that launch is over

request.description: Drops the record place_launch filed. Sent when the loading screen for it ends, however it ended: the window arrived, the process died, the wait ran out, the display was unplugged. Naming a launch that was never filed, or one already dropped, does nothing.

arg.name: launch
arg.summary: the number place_launch was given

request.name: set_output_overview

description.summary: enter or leave the window overview on one display

request.description:
While the overview is on, the compositor stops drawing that display's windows at their real geometry and instead animates each one into a card slot, laid out by the algorithm both sides share (the shell and the compositor are built from the same crate, so the slots the shell decorates are exactly the slots the compositor fills).
The shell draws everything else of the overview — the menu beside the cards, the selection frame and the titles — on its own layer surface, transparent where the cards show through. Leaving the overview animates every window back to where it was.
Enabling it on a second display implicitly leaves it on the first: the overview belongs to the display the user is driving.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to change

arg.name: enabled
arg.summary: 1 to enter the overview, 0 to leave it

request.name: set_overview_selection

description.summary: which overview card the shell has selected

request.description:
Tells the compositor which card the user is on, counted over the shell's full card list — every window plus the trailing start-screen card. The row scrolls to keep that card visible, and the scroll position is derived from this index by the shared layout, so saying the selection is what keeps the two processes scrolling as one.
Meaningful only while the overview is on; harmless otherwise.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: index
arg.summary: selected card, 0-based

request.name: activate_window

description.summary: bring one window to the front and focus it

request.description:
Raises and focuses the window named by an output_window event. The shell sends this when a card is chosen in the overview; it is how the overview doubles as a window switcher.
Silently ignored when the window is gone — it may have closed between the event and the choice.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the window, from output_window

request.name: activate_window_from

description.summary: bring a window back, growing out of where it was asked for

request.description:
As activate_window, and in addition flies the window in from the given rectangle — in the display's logical pixels — over the same flight the overview's cards use.
This is what a tile press does when the application it names is already running. What the user asked for is not a copy of the application but the one they left, and what they should see is that one arriving: the window itself growing out of the tile, the way an application already in memory opens on a phone. A splash panel with an icon and a spinner would say the opposite — that something is being loaded — and it would be a lie in the one case where the application is demonstrably already there.
Only the compositor can do this, because only the compositor has the window's pixels. It draws the flight above everything else on that display, the shell's own surface included, so the start screen the window grows out of stays behind it for the whole of the flight instead of being taken away first.
The rectangle is a starting point, not a crop: the window keeps its aspect ratio and is fitted inside, exactly as a card is. Sending a rectangle that is empty, or naming a window that is gone, is the same as activate_window on its own.

arg.summary: the window, from output_window

arg.name: x
arg.summary: left edge of the rectangle to grow from

arg.name: y
arg.summary: top edge of the rectangle to grow from

arg.name: width
arg.summary: width of that rectangle

arg.name: height
arg.summary: height of that rectangle

request.name: kill_window

description.summary: end one window's application outright

request.description:
Ends the application behind the window named by an output_window event.
Unlike close_foreground this is not a request the client can refuse, prompt about or ignore: the shell's overlay is the console's way out of an application that is not answering, and an application that puts up a "save your work?" dialog behind an overlay the user has just dismissed is indistinguishable from one that has hung.
What it ends is the application, not the window's process — those are not always the same thing, and a supervised helper killed on its own is simply rebuilt, window and all, by whatever was supervising it. The compositor resolves the application from the window's client credentials, which for an X11 window means the window's own pid rather than Xwayland's, and reaches the rest of it through the process tree. An application whose lifetime belongs to a session or container outside that tree is ended the way that session ends.
The application is asked before it is ended, and ended shortly after whether or not it answered. Nothing about that is negotiable from the client side; the pause exists so that an application which does answer can finish writing, not so that it can decline.
Silently ignored when the window is gone. An application that cannot be identified at all — one forwarded from another machine, which is not this session's to end — is asked to close instead.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the window, from output_window

request.name: move_window_to_output

description.summary: move one window to another display

request.description:
Moves the window named by an output_window event to a different display, and makes it that display's window: it is re-tiled across the new screen, raised there, and belongs to it from then on — an application pinned to the display it opened on is pinned to this one instead.
Only the compositor can do it. The shell knows which displays exist and which window the user picked, but a window's place in the layout is the compositor's, and a client cannot be asked to move itself: it does not know where the other display is, and under this layout it does not choose its own geometry in the first place.
Keyboard focus is deliberately left alone. This is sent from an overlay that is holding the keyboard on the display the user is standing on, and a move is not a request to go and look at the other screen.
Silently ignored when the window is gone, when the output is gone, and when the window is already on that display.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the window, from output_window

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to move it to

request.name: capture_window

description.summary: write one window's pixels to a PNG file

request.description:
Captures the window named by an output_window event — its own contents at its own size, with nothing in front of it and no wallpaper behind — and writes it to `path` as a PNG.
Only the compositor has those pixels. A client cannot photograph another client's window, and the shell cannot photograph the window it is drawn over even when that window is on screen: what it holds is a layer surface of its own.
The path is the shell's to choose, and is passed rather than worked out here, because where a user's pictures go is a question about the user's session and not about the display server. It must be absolute, and its directory must already exist — the compositor creates neither. Nothing is written anywhere else: a relative path, or one that cannot be written, is refused.
The answer comes back as window_captured, always: a shell that has told the user it took a screenshot has to be able to tell them where it went, or that it did not happen.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the window, from output_window

arg.name: path
arg.summary: absolute path of the PNG file to write

request.name: move_pointer

description.summary: move the pointer, as a mouse would

request.description:
Moves the seat's pointer by a relative amount, in logical pixels, and delivers the motion to whatever is under it — including the relative stream a game with a locked pointer reads its camera from.
A console has a controller and no mouse, and an application that wants a pointer cannot be given one by the shell: wl_pointer belongs to the seat, and only the compositor may speak for the seat. Neither can the shell simply move a cursor of its own, because the point is to reach the *application* — a stick that moved a drawing on the shell's own surface would click on nothing.
The shell reads the controller straight from /dev/input, which is what lets it drive this while a fullscreen application holds the keyboard, and turns it on per application: a game already using the right stick for its camera must not have it taken away by a shell that thinks the stick is a mouse.
Deltas accumulate; sending one every controller poll is the intended shape. It is ignored while no application window exists, so a shell that leaves the stick on cannot walk the pointer across an empty desktop.
The pointer stays inside that application. A mouse belongs to the session and may be pushed onto any display in it; this stick was turned on for one window, and there is nothing outside that window it was aimed at — least of all a second screen, where the user cannot see the cursor arrive. So movement is held inside the window the compositor is delivering it to: the topmost application on the display the shell says it is being driven on, which is the same window set_driven_output and output_app_id already agree about.
And a pointer left outside it is fetched back. A session has a mouse as well, and a mouse may leave the cursor anywhere; the first movement after that puts it at the nearest point of the window, so that the stick always means something. That fetch is delivered as motion but withheld from the relative stream — it is a pointer being retrieved, not a hand moving a mouse.

arg.name: dx
arg.summary: horizontal movement, logical pixels

arg.name: dy
arg.summary: vertical movement, logical pixels

request.name: pointer_button

description.summary: press or release a pointer button

request.description:
Presses or releases one of the seat's pointer buttons where the pointer currently is, exactly as a mouse button does — including raising and focusing what it lands on. Where it is: this does not fetch the pointer back the way move_pointer does, because the cursor the user is looking at is what a click has to answer to.
A pointer that cannot click is a cursor drawing, so this comes with move_pointer rather than after it. The button is a Linux input code (BTN_LEFT is 0x110), which is what wl_pointer itself carries.
Ignored while no application window exists, for the same reason move_pointer is.

arg.name: button
arg.summary: Linux button code, as wl_pointer reports it

arg.name: state
arg.summary: pressed or released

request.name: scroll_pointer

description.summary: scroll where the pointer is

request.description:
Scrolls whatever is under the pointer, as a wheel or a touchpad does, by an amount in logical pixels. Positive is the direction a wheel turned away from the user scrolls in: down, and right.
A pointer that can only be moved and clicked leaves half of what a mouse does out, and the half that a page of settings, a browser or a file list needs most. The shell sends this from the stick and the D-pad the pointer is *not* being aimed with, which are the controls it has already stopped using for its own navigation while an application is in front.
It is continuous rather than a count of wheel notches, because a stick is: it is pushed further to scroll faster, exactly as a touchpad is dragged further. The compositor describes it to clients as the continuous axis source it is.
Ignored while no application window exists, for the same reason move_pointer is.

arg.name: dx
arg.summary: horizontal scroll, logical pixels

arg.name: dy
arg.summary: vertical scroll, logical pixels

enum.name: button_state

description.summary: whether a pointer button is down

enum.description: The same two values wl_pointer uses, so a shell forwarding a button it received does not have to translate one enumeration into another.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: the button is not pressed

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: the button is pressed

request.name: keyboard_key

description.summary: press or release a key on the seat's keyboard

request.description:
Presses or releases a key on the seat's keyboard, delivered to whatever holds keyboard focus exactly as a key on a real keyboard would be — through the compositor's own keymap, so the client sees the keysym its layout gives that key.
This is not a way to type. A shell with an on-screen keyboard already has zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1 or zwp_input_method_v2 for that, and either is the right thing for text. It is here for the keys that are *not* text: the arrows, which are how a list, a menu or a document is moved through, and which a console shell has a D-pad for and nothing else to do with while the pointer is being aimed with the other stick.
The key is a Linux input code (KEY_LEFT is 105), for the same reason pointer_button carries one: it is what the seat's keyboard is fed from, and translating a keysym back into a keycode means guessing at the layout the compositor is holding.
Held keys repeat in the client, from the repeat rate the seat already advertises, so a direction is a press when it goes down and a release when it comes up rather than a press for every repeat. A shell that stops sending must release what it has pressed; the compositor releases anything left held if the shell disconnects, but nothing else can know the difference between a held key and a shell that stopped talking.
Ignored while no application window exists, for the same reason move_pointer is.

arg.summary: Linux key code, as wl_keyboard reports it

arg.name: state
arg.summary: pressed or released

enum.name: key_state

description.summary: whether a key is down

enum.description: The same two values wl_keyboard uses.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: the key is not pressed

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: the key is pressed

request.name: set_output_hdr

description.summary: drive one display in HDR, and say how

request.description:
Puts a display into high dynamic range — the connector is told the signal is BT.2020 with the ST 2084 (PQ) transfer function, and the compositor's own output is re-encoded to match — or takes it back out of it.
Everything about this belongs to the compositor rather than to the shell. The colour pipeline that does the re-encoding is the CRTC's, the metadata that tells the display what it is being sent is an infoframe only a modesetting client may attach, and both have to survive the shell being restarted. What the shell owns is the *decision*, which is why this is a request and not a client-side setting: it is a page in the Settings column, and the compositor is what carries it out.
The four values are sent together because they are one pipeline and are applied as one commit. A shell that only wants to change the brightness still sends all four, which is also what makes this idempotent — an unchanged set is recognised and costs nothing.
sdr_brightness is the luminance the display is asked to give plain white. Everything on screen is SDR content, so this is the single control that decides whether the session comes out dim or blinding; 100 cd/m² is the reference the sRGB standard names and roughly what an SDR display in a lit room does.
srgb_intensity says how far sRGB's colours are stretched on their way into BT.2020's much wider gamut. At 0 the conversion is exact and the session looks the way it did in SDR. At 100 the numbers are passed through untouched, so sRGB's red is displayed as BT.2020's red and everything comes out far more saturated — the "vivid" setting a television ships in. In between is a blend of the two.
peak_brightness is the luminance declared to the display as the brightest the content will reach. 0 means "whatever the display says it can do", read from its EDID, which is the right answer unless the user knows their display overstates it.
Ignored, with the settings remembered, when the output cannot be driven in HDR: see the output_hdr event, which is how a shell knows whether to offer this at all. Silently ignored when the output is gone.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to configure

arg.name: enabled
arg.summary: 1 to drive the display in HDR, 0 for SDR

arg.name: sdr_brightness
arg.summary: reference white for SDR content, cd/m²

arg.name: srgb_intensity
arg.summary: how far sRGB colour is stretched towards BT.2020, 0 to 100

arg.name: peak_brightness
arg.summary: peak luminance to declare, cd/m²; 0 for the display's own

request.name: set_output_mode

description.summary: drive one display at a different resolution

request.description:
Asks the compositor to change a display's mode: the resolution it is scanned out at, and the rate it is refreshed at.
A mode is a modesetting client's to choose for the same reason HDR is. The connector's mode list comes off the hardware, the change is an atomic commit on a CRTC nobody else may touch, and everything on that display — every window, every layer surface, the shell's own bar — has to be reconfigured to the new size afterwards. What the shell owns is the decision.
width and height are the mode's own pixel dimensions, before any scale or transform the output carries: they are what the connector lists, and what an output_mode event reported.
refresh is in mHz, as the mode list gives it, so a 59.94 Hz mode is 59940. 0 asks for the fastest mode of that size, which is what a shell that only cares about the resolution should send. Anything else is matched to the nearest refresh the display offers at that size, so a rate that is no longer in the list — the display was swapped for another behind the same connector — still lands on something rather than being dropped.
Ignored when nothing of that size exists, when the display is gone, and on a backend with no connectors to set a mode on: a nested session is the size of its window. In all three the display keeps the mode it has, and the output_mode events say so — a shell should mark what those report rather than what it asked for.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to change

arg.name: width
arg.summary: mode width in pixels

arg.name: height
arg.summary: mode height in pixels

arg.name: refresh
arg.summary: refresh in mHz; 0 for the fastest of that size

enum.name: transform

description.summary: how a display's picture is turned

enum.description:
The same eight values as wl_output.transform, with the same numbers and the same meanings, so a shell that reads one does not have to translate it into the other.
Four of them are rotations and four are the same rotations with the picture flipped about a vertical axis first. A display standing on its side wants a rotation; the flipped values are for a picture reaching the eye through a mirror, and a shell has no reason to offer them unless it knows there is one.

entry.summary: no rotation
a quarter turn
upside down
a quarter turn the other way

entry.name: flipped_90
entry.summary: mirrored, then a quarter turn

entry.name: flipped_180
entry.summary: mirrored, then upside down

entry.name: flipped_270
entry.summary: mirrored, then a quarter turn the other way

request.name: set_output_transform

description.summary: turn one display's picture

request.description:
Asks the compositor to draw a display's picture turned: a screen standing on its side is given a quarter turn so that what it shows stands up with it.
It belongs to the compositor for the plainest of the reasons a mode does: everything on that display is laid out in the space the turn creates. A quarter turn swaps the display's logical width and height, which moves the outputs laid out beside it, re-arranges every layer surface anchored to it — the shell's own bar included — and re-tiles every window on it. A client can no more do that than it can choose its own geometry under this layout.
Unlike a mode this is the compositor's own rendering rather than the connector's: the picture is composited turned and scanned out at the mode's own pixels, so every display can be turned and no display has a list of turns it will accept. What varies is only whether the compositor owns the picture at all — see the output_transform event, which is how a shell knows whether to offer this.
Silently ignored when the output is gone, when the value is not one of the eight, and on a display the compositor does not report a transform for. In each case the display keeps the orientation it has, and the output_transform event says so — a shell should mark what that reports rather than what it asked for.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to turn

arg.name: transform
arg.summary: how to turn its picture

request.name: hide_pointer

description.summary: the user has picked up something that is not the pointer

request.description:
Takes the cursor off screen, exactly as the compositor does by itself when a key is pressed on a keyboard it can see.
It needs asking for because a controller is not a seat device: the shell reads it straight from /dev/input, so a user who has put the mouse down and picked a gamepad up leaves no trace the compositor could notice. This is the shell saying so on their behalf.
The cursor comes back the moment the pointer next moves — a mouse, a touchpad, or the shell's own stick pointer. There is deliberately no request to put it back: a cursor that could be summoned without being moved would appear somewhere the user is not looking, which is the thing hiding it was for.
A shell driving the pointer with a stick should not send this for the buttons that stick is clicking with. Those are the pointer being used, not put down.

request.name: capture_output

description.summary: write one display's pixels to a PNG file

request.description:
Photographs a whole display — everything on it, in the order it is drawn: the wallpaper, every application window, the shell's own bar or overlay over them — and writes it to `path` as a PNG.
This is capture_window's companion and not a wider version of it. That one answers "what does this application look like", and cuts the window out of its surroundings to do it. This one answers "what is on this screen", which is a picture of the composite and can be taken of a display with nothing running on it at all.
The picture has as many pixels as the display is driven at, turned the way the display is turned. The pointer is left out: the cursor is drawn by the compositor rather than being part of any surface, it is not on screen at all while the session is being driven from a controller, and an arrow burnt into a screenshot cannot be taken back out of it.
The path is the shell's to choose, on the same terms as capture_window: absolute, into a directory that already exists, and refused otherwise.
The answer comes back as output_captured, always, for the reason window_captured always answers.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to photograph

arg.name: path
arg.summary: absolute path of the PNG file to write

request.name: ask_to_share

description.summary: ask the user whether an application may see a display

request.description:
Puts a question to the session shell: this application wants to share a screen — may it, and which one? The answer comes back as share_answered, always, so a portal waiting on it is never left waiting.
Sent by the session's desktop portal rather than by the shell. Screen sharing is not something an application does for itself: it asks xdg-desktop-portal, which asks the portal backend, which is a client of this compositor like any other — and the one thing that client cannot do is draw. Only the shell can, and only the compositor can reach the shell while a fullscreen application holds the screen.
id is the asking client's own number for this question, unique among the questions it currently has outstanding, and is quoted back in the answer. app_id is what the application asking calls itself, for the shell to name in the question; it may be empty, and a shell should then say so rather than showing an empty name.
The question goes to every other client bound to this interface, and never back to the one that asked. In a running session that is the shell, which is the only client that has anywhere to put it.
Refused outright when nobody can be asked — no shell has bound this interface, or none new enough to hear the question — because a screen shared without anybody being asked is the thing this request exists to prevent.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the asking client's number for this question

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: what the application asking calls itself

request.name: answer_share

description.summary: answer a share_request

request.description:
The shell's answer to one share_request: the display the user chose, or nothing at all, which is the user saying no.
Answering a question nobody asked, or one that has already been answered, is ignored — a client that has gone away takes its question with it.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the question, from share_request

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display that may be shared, or nothing for a refusal

request.name: keep_out_of_sight

description.summary: run this application without ever showing it

request.description:
Names an application whose windows are never to reach the screen. They are not drawn, they are not announced as windows on any display, they are never given the keyboard, and the pointer passes through them. The application itself is untouched: it is mapped, configured and drawing exactly as it would be, and it is simply never looked at.
This is for a program the shell drives rather than presents. The Steam client is the one that needs it — the shell signs it in, starts games through it and reads its library, all of which it does perfectly well with nobody watching, but which it punctuates with windows of its own: a "starting game" dialog over the shell's own loading screen, and its whole storefront raised on top of a game that is trying to start. From the user's side those are the shell failing to hide its plumbing.
Hiding is the shell's to give back. A user who asks for Steam's own window — to verify a game's files, or to see the client itself — is asking for exactly the thing this suppresses, so the shell sends this again with hidden set to zero before asking Steam for it.
Sending it for an application with windows already on screen takes them off it, and giving sight back puts them where they were. An empty app_id names nothing and is ignored, rather than hiding every window that never set one.

arg.summary: what the application calls itself

request.name: let_this_window_be_seen

description.summary: one exception to keep_out_of_sight

request.description:
Lets a single window of a hidden application through, without giving the application itself back. It is drawn, listed, focusable and clickable exactly as any other window; everything else the application owns stays where keep_out_of_sight put it.
This exists because a program the shell drives rather than presents still stops and asks things. Valve's client is the one that needs it: it signs itself in, fetches games and reads a library with nobody watching, and then puts up a window that nothing will get past until somebody answers it — a sign-in, an agreement, a licence key, a parental code, a conflict between two saves. Hidden, that window is a session where Steam has silently stopped and the screen says nothing.
The compositor takes no view of which window that is. It says what it is hiding, through unseen_window, and the shell — which knows what it asked the application for and what it is still waiting on — decides.
The exception is on the window, not on the application, and it lasts as long as the window does: a compositor that has forgotten a window has forgotten this about it too, and an id reused for another window starts hidden like everything else. Naming a window that does not exist, or one whose application is not hidden at all, does nothing.

arg.summary: the window, from unseen_window

request.name: set_output_night_light

description.summary: warm one display's picture, or stop

request.description:
Puts a night light — a blue light filter — on one display: everything it shows is tinted towards the given colour temperature, so a screen looked at in the evening is not a daylight-white one.
It is the CRTC's gamma ramp, which is why it is the compositor's to carry out for the reason HDR is: the ramp is a KMS property on a pipe only a modesetting client may commit to, it acts on everything scanned out rather than on anything a client drew, and it has to survive the shell being restarted.
temperature is in kelvin, and lower is warmer: 6500 K is ordinary daylight white and is what an untinted display already shows, 4000 K is an evening setting, and 2000 K is candlelight. It is clamped into the range this compositor can encode rather than refused, because a display left at some other temperature is a worse way to report a number out of range than the nearest one that means something.
The two values go together because they are one ramp and are applied as one commit, which is also what makes this idempotent: an unchanged pair is recognised and costs nothing.
*When* the light is on is the shell's, not the compositor's. A schedule is a clock and a time zone, and both belong to the session that has a Settings page to set them on — so the shell sends enabled = 1 when its own schedule says the light should be burning now, and 0 when it should not.
This composes with set_output_hdr rather than competing with it. On a display being driven in HDR the tint is folded into the same ramp that does the PQ encoding, so both are in force at once and neither undoes the other.
Ignored, with the setting remembered, when the display has no gamma ramp to warm: see the output_night_light event, which is how a shell knows whether to offer this at all. Silently ignored when the output is gone.

arg.summary: the display to warm

arg.name: enabled
arg.summary: 1 to warm the picture now, 0 to leave it alone

arg.name: temperature
arg.summary: colour temperature in kelvin; lower is warmer, 6500 is daylight

request.name: set_output_place

description.summary: put one display at this place in the layout

request.description:
Moves a display along the row the compositor lays its displays out in: the screen the user calls their first one becomes place 0, the one beside it place 1, and so on.
It belongs to the compositor because the arrangement is the desktop's own shape. Where each display sits decides where a pointer crossing an edge comes out, which display a window is tiled onto, and the coordinates every client on the session is told about — none of which a client can be allowed to compute for itself.
place is counted from zero, and it is an index into the displays the output_place event reports rather than into every display connected. A display the compositor does not place — one pinned by its own config, or a session mirroring every screen onto the same region — takes no part in either.
The display already at that place takes the one being vacated: this is a trade, not an insertion. That is what makes it composable, which is what a shell restoring a whole arrangement needs — sending one of these per display, in ascending place, leaves every display where it was asked for, because each request fixes one display and can only disturb a place no later request names.
Silently ignored when the output is gone, when place is past the end of the list, and when this display is not one the compositor places. In each case the arrangement is left as it is, and the output_place events say so — a shell should mark what those report rather than what it asked for.
Not remembered by the compositor, unlike a mode or an orientation. Both of those are written down because the alternative is a modeset a second after login, which is a black screen; an arrangement costs a relayout, which at login is a desktop with nothing on it yet. So the shell keeps this one, and sends it when it connects.

arg.summary: the display to move

arg.name: place
arg.summary: the place it should take, counted from zero

request.name: controller_used

description.summary: the user has picked the controller back up

request.description:
Says that a button was pressed or a stick pushed on a controller, which the compositor never sees: a shell reads its pads straight from /dev/input, so a user who has put the keyboard down and taken a gamepad up leaves no trace here at all. This is the counterpart of hide_pointer, one step further out — that one says the mouse has been put down, this one says the keyboard has.
It arms the typed event again. That event is sent once and then held back until this request arrives, so the two together are one message per handover rather than one per keystroke.
A shell that never sends it is told about the first key pressed after it bound this interface and about nothing after that.

request.name: set_application_scale

description.summary: how large applications draw themselves

request.description:
Sets how much larger than life every application on the session draws its own interface: at 150 a window's text, buttons and margins come out half again the size they would at 100, without losing a pixel of sharpness.
It is the compositor's because it is not a filter over a picture — it is a *smaller window told to draw at more pixels*. Each application is configured with a logical size the given factor smaller than the screen and told, over wp_fractional_scale_v1, that its scale is that much higher; a client that honours the two renders exactly as many pixels as the display has, and the compositor puts them on it one for one. So nothing is stretched and nothing is resampled: the interface is drawn bigger, in the same way it is drawn bigger on a high-density laptop panel. A client that ignores the scale is drawn at the size it chose and enlarged, which is the same graceful answer such a client gets from every other compositor.
scale is in per cent of natural size, and 100 — one to one — is the floor. Below it an application would be asked to draw more of its interface than the display has room for, which is not what a screen looked at from a sofa wants and is not what this is for; a smaller number is clamped up to 100 rather than refused, as an out-of-range colour temperature is clamped, because an application shown at some unrelated size is a worse way to report a bad number than the nearest one that means something. The ceiling is likewise a clamp.
Applications only, and Wayland ones. The shell's own surfaces are untouched — it is not an application, it draws itself against the display it was given, and a shell that changed size with this setting would take the Settings page the user is looking at with it. Windows under Xwayland are untouched too: X11 has no per-surface scale to be told about, so the only thing that could be done to those windows is to magnify pixels that are already drawn, and a blurred window is not what somebody asking for a larger one asked for.
Session-wide, and since version 43 the *default* rather than the whole answer: set_output_application_scale says it for one display, and this is what every display a shell has not named draws at. A shell that sends only this one gets what it always got, on every screen it has and on every screen plugged in afterwards.
Not remembered by the compositor. An application is started by the shell, always after the shell has connected and said what this is, so there is no window that could come up at the wrong size while the two agree — and the shell has the Settings page it was set on, which is where a preference belongs.

arg.name: scale
arg.summary: per cent of natural size; 100 is one to one, and the floor

request.name: set_output_application_scale

description.summary: how large applications draw themselves on one display

request.description:
The same setting as set_application_scale, for one display: every application tiled onto this screen draws its own interface this much larger than life, and the displays beside it are left as they are.
Per display because a screen is looked at from where it stands. A television across a room and the panel on the desk in front of it want different answers, and a session with one answer for both had to be wrong about one of them — which is what this splits. The setting is still about a person and a distance; what changes is that a person has a different distance to each of their screens.
Which means a window carries its display's answer, and a window moved between two displays is configured again for the one it lands on. That is the same relayout as a window moved between screens of different sizes: it is the display it is on that decides how much room it is given.
scale is in per cent of natural size, clamped into the same range set_application_scale is clamped into and for the same reason: 100 is one to one and the floor, the ceiling is as far as this goes, and a number outside them is brought to the nearer end rather than refused.
What it does to a window, what it deliberately leaves alone — the shell's own surfaces, and anything under Xwayland — and why the compositor writes none of it down are all as set_application_scale describes. This is that setting with a display named.
A display nobody has named here draws at whatever set_application_scale last said, which is natural size until a shell says otherwise. Sent for a display and then for the same display again with a different number, the last one stands; there is no request to go back to the session's default, because a shell that wants that sends it as this display's.
Silently ignored when the output is gone.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display whose applications are being sized

arg.name: scale
arg.summary: per cent of natural size; 100 is one to one, and the floor

request.name: set_application_resolution

description.summary: how many pixels one application draws

request.description:
Sets the number of pixels one named application draws its picture at, whatever the display it ends up on is showing. At 1280x720 on a 4K screen the application lays itself out in 1280x720, renders 1280x720 pixels, and the compositor puts that picture over the whole display.
The opposite bargain from set_application_scale, and deliberately so. That one asks for a *larger interface at the display's own sharpness*: the window is made smaller and the client is told over wp_fractional_scale_v1 to fill it with as many pixels as the screen has. This one asks for *fewer pixels*: the window is made smaller and the client is told nothing extra, so it draws exactly the picture that was asked for and that picture is enlarged onto the screen. It is what a console means by a game's resolution — the work of drawing a frame is cut to a quarter and the frame still covers the television — and it is why the two cannot be one request with a different unit.
app_id is the name a window calls itself by: an xdg_toplevel's app_id, or an X11 window's class. A shell that knows an application under several names sends this once per name; the compositor compares them whole, ignoring case, and does not guess at what a name is short for. An empty app_id is refused — nothing can be filed under nothing, and a window that named itself nothing must not inherit a setting meant for another.
Xwayland windows are included, unlike set_application_scale. There the exclusion is honest, because there is no per-surface scale to tell an X11 client about and all that could be done is to magnify what it already drew. Here magnifying is the whole request: an X11 client configured at 1280x720 really does draw 1280x720 pixels, and drawing them over the display is what was asked for rather than a poor substitute for it.
width and height are in pixels, and 0x0 means the display's own — which is the answer for an application nobody has chosen for, and the way a choice is taken back. A size larger than a display in either direction is not carried out on that display: the window there is given the display's own size, because what the size would ask for is a picture shrunk to fit, which is a different setting from this one and is not one this compositor offers. It is kept rather than refused all the same, since a session with two screens of different sizes is one where the same application can honour it on one of them and not the other.
A size that does not have the display's shape is fitted inside it, by whichever of the two directions runs out first, and the window is left in the display's own corner. A shell is expected to offer sizes that share the shape of the screen they will be drawn on, so this is the answer to a mistake rather than a feature: the picture stays the shape the application drew it, which is the one thing worth protecting.
Not remembered by the compositor, for the reason set_application_scale is not: every application on this session is started by the shell, the shell says this before it starts one, and the shell has the menu it was chosen on. A window already on screen when this arrives is configured again at once, which is what makes the setting mean something while somebody is looking at the application it is about.

arg.summary: the name the application's windows call themselves by

arg.name: width
arg.summary: pixels across, or 0 with height for the display's own

arg.name: height
arg.summary: pixels down, or 0 with width for the display's own

request.name: cover_in_black

description.summary: fade every display to black, or bring it back

request.description:
Draws one black sheet over each display — over every application, over the shell's own surfaces, over the cursor — and fades it in over about half a second. Sent again with covered set to 0, it fades back off.
This is what a console does on its way out. The session shell asks for it when the user chooses to turn the machine off, and only then does it run the command that ends the session: a shutdown that cut straight to black would look like a display losing its signal, and there is no difference on screen between that and a crash.
It has to be the compositor's sheet rather than the shell's. The shell draws one surface per display and an application in front of it owns the screen; a shell that blacked out its own surfaces would darken the display the menu was on and leave a game running on the other one.
While the curtain is anything but fully up the session takes no input at all — not the keyboard, not the pointer, not a touch, and not the compositor's own bindings. A machine on its way down must not be driven, and half a second is long enough to press something in. That includes the bindings that would leave the session, so a client which asks for this and then does not go must take it back up again; see screen_is_black for the answer that says it is safe to leave.
The pixels are the only thing this touches. Applications are not stopped, not resized and not told anything: they are simply not visible, and what they were doing when the machine went is what they were doing.

arg.name: covered
arg.summary: 1 to fade to black, 0 to fade back off it

request.name: cover_output_in_black

description.summary: fade one display to black, or bring it back

request.description:
The same black sheet cover_in_black draws, over one display instead of over the session, and with none of that request's authority over the rest of it.
This is what a screen nobody is looking at rests behind while a game is being played on another one. An OLED panel left showing a still picture keeps it: the start screen's bar is in the same place every second it is up, and a second screen left on it for the length of an evening's play is the worst case there is. So the shell asks for the black once that display has been left alone, and asks for it back the moment the user goes near it again.
It has to be the compositor's sheet for the reason the session's is: the shell owns one surface per display, and everything else on that display — an application in front of it, the cursor over the top — belongs to somebody else. A shell blacking out its own surfaces would leave a paused film and a pointer lit on the screen it was resting.
Unlike cover_in_black this takes nothing away. The session goes on taking input while it is down, on this display and on every other: the whole point is that moving the pointer onto a resting screen brings it back, and a curtain that swallowed the movement could never be lifted by it. Nothing is hidden from any client either — no window is told anything, resized, or stopped — because a display resting is a fact about the panel and not about what is running on it.
The fade is a second going down and a quarter of a second coming back up, eased at both ends, and reversible from wherever it has got to: a pointer that arrives halfway through brings the screen back from half black rather than from all of it.
Asking for what a display is already doing costs nothing and does not restart the fade. Silently ignored when the output is gone.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display to rest

arg.name: covered
arg.summary: 1 to fade to black, 0 to fade back off it

request.name: keep_awake

description.summary: this application is playing something; do not stop it

request.description:
Names an application that must go on running even with nothing of it on screen. Everything else about it is unchanged: it is not drawn, it is not given the keyboard, and it is not put in front of anything. It is simply not stopped.
An application nobody can see is stopped outright — that is what keeps a covered game from going on playing its music into the room — and the one thing that rule is wrong about is an application whose whole purpose is the sound it is making. A game covered by the start screen should fall silent. Music the user put on should not, and neither should the stream they are listening to while they play.
The compositor cannot tell those apart. The difference is not in the window, not in the process tree and not in the audio: a game's soundtrack and an album are both a program feeding a sink. It is on the session bus, where a media player says what it is playing and whether it is playing it, and the shell is the half of this session that is on a bus at all.
So the shell decides and this carries the answer. What it means by it is deliberately narrow — an application that both announces itself as a media player and is audibly playing, which no game does — and it is held for a short while after the sound stops, because the silence between two tracks is not the end of the music and an application stopped in that gap would never reach the next one.
Sent again with awake set to zero when that stops being true. An application named here while it is already stopped is started again at once. An empty app_id names nothing and is ignored.

arg.summary: what the application calls itself

arg.name: awake

enum.description:
Three sizes rather than a number of pixels, for the reason the shell offers three: what the user is choosing is how much of the screen they are willing to give up, and a display's own size is the compositor's to read. Each is a share of the display's width, so the same choice is the same fraction of a laptop panel and of a television across the room.
How *tall* the window is at that width is the window's own business. The compositor asks it what shape it wants to be — a configure carrying no size, which is xdg-shell for "choose one" — and follows the answer, so a video that is four to three is drawn four to three and one stood on its end is drawn standing on its end. It goes on following it, so a video swapped for one of another shape in the same window is drawn in the new one.

The four corners, and only the four corners. A floating window on a console is not dragged anywhere — there is no pointer in the user's hand to drag it with — so what a page can honestly offer is the corner it starts in, and every corner is the same distance from the edges.
A second such window, opened while the first is still up, stands below it in a column from that corner rather than on top of it: two of them in one place is one window with something wrong with it.

request.name: set_picture_in_picture

description.summary: whether a video floats over everything, and where

request.description:
Sets what the compositor does with a window a browser has put into picture-in-picture: the small always-on-top player somebody keeps a match or a lecture in while they use the machine for something else.
Such a window says what it is in its title, and says it in the one string every browser that has the feature agrees on — "Picture-in-Picture". That is what the compositor matches, and it is the whole of the test. It cannot be an app_id: the window belongs to the browser and calls itself by the browser's name, which is also what the window the video came out of calls itself.
A window that answers to it is taken out of the layout every other window is under. It is not maximized, it is not given the keyboard, it is not listed to the shell as something to switch to or to close, and it is drawn in front of everything the session has — over a fullscreen game, over the shell's own start screen, and over the guide, which is the one surface nothing else in this protocol is allowed in front of. That is what the feature is: a window that is still there while the user does something else. It is drawn with a hairline surround and its own corners rounded, held off the edges of the screen by the radius the shell gives its menus, so that what floats over the session is spaced the way the session is — and it is drawn *only* there, and *all* of there: a client that puts its own drop shadow outside its window, or that will not take the size it is given, is clipped to that shape rather than allowed to spill past it, and whatever it leaves uncovered inside that shape is filled rather than left to show the session through.
enabled turns the whole of that off again. A compositor told zero treats such a window as the application window it otherwise is — maximized, listed, focusable — which is the layout this shell had before it could be asked, and is the honest answer for somebody who does not want a video following them around.
The three arguments arrive together because they are one rectangle. A size sent without its corner, or a corner without its size, would move the window twice for one press.
size and place describe where such a window *starts*. A compositor may let the user move and resize one by hand — this one does, with a mouse — and a window that has been moved keeps where it was put rather than following these: it is out of the corner and out of the column below it, and the place it stood in is free for the next window that floats. What puts it back is this request arriving with a different size or corner, which is the user saying on the page where they want their videos.
Not remembered by the compositor. The shell says what this is as soon as it connects, before any application exists to put a video in — the same bargain set_application_scale is under, and for the same reason: the preference belongs to the page it was set on.

request.name: pip_menu_command

description.summary: carry out a row of the floating window's menu

request.description:
Sent when the user chooses one of the rows of the menu a pip_menu event asked for. Only the rows a client cannot carry out itself arrive here — see the pip_command enum, which is the whole list.
move and resize hand the pointer to the compositor: it is put on the window (in the middle of it, or on the corner being pulled), the window follows it, and the next click leaves the window where it is. Nothing is held down throughout, because nothing was held down to begin with — the user let go of the button that chose the row. A click of any other button puts the window back where it was.
close asks the window to close, exactly as close_foreground does, and is deliberately not close_window: that one ends the *application*, and the application here is a browser with the rest of somebody's session in it. What this ends is one video in one corner, which the browser answers by putting it back in the page it came from.
Silently ignored when the window is gone, when it is not floating any more, or when the number is not a command this compositor knows.

arg.name: command

request.name: pip_select

description.summary: which floating window the shell's own controls are on

request.description:
Names the floating window the user has the directions on, so the compositor can mark it. A console has no pointer: the only way to say which of two videos in a corner a button is about is to select one and show which one is selected, and only the compositor can show it — the window is drawn in front of every surface this shell owns, so a mark drawn by the shell would be behind the thing it is marking.
An id of zero selects nothing, which is the resting state and the one to go back to whenever the shell stops offering the controls: the overlay closing, the display being handed to another screen, the window going away.
accent is the colour to mark it in, as 0xRRGGBB. It travels with the selection because it is the shell's, not the compositor's: it is the accent the user chose, it changes while they choose it, and a compositor that read it out of the shell's settings for itself would be a second copy of that answer, drifting.
Silently ignored for a window that is gone or is not floating.

arg.summary: the window, from pip_window, or 0 for none

arg.name: accent
arg.summary: the colour to mark it in, 0xRRGGBB

request.name: pip_grab

description.summary: take hold of a floating window without a pointer

request.description:
Starts moving or resizing a floating window on a controller's behalf. The window follows the deltas of pip_drag from here until pip_drop ends it, exactly as it follows a pointer that has hold of it — same arithmetic, same limits, same detaching from the corner it started in.
Nothing is warped and nothing is pressed: no pointer is involved at any point, and whatever the pointer is over goes on hearing about it. That is the whole difference between this and the move and resize rows of pip_menu_command, which are the same two acts done with a mouse.
A second grab while one is already under way is ignored, as is one on a window that is gone or not floating. There is one hand on one window at a time on this session, whichever control it belongs to.

Moves or resizes the window pip_grab took hold of by a relative amount, in logical pixels. Deltas accumulate; sending one every controller poll is the intended shape, as it is for move_pointer.
Each step is measured from where the window is *now* rather than from where the grab started, so a stick held into the edge of the display does not build up travel the user has to push back out of before the window moves again.
For a resize the delta is read as the pull on the corner the compositor chose, and the window keeps the shape its own client asked to be: one of the two numbers is what the stick said and the other is what that shape makes of it.

Ends the grab. keep of 1 leaves the window where the drags left it; 0 puts it back where it was when the grab started — which is a state and not only a rectangle, so a window that was standing in the corner the settings put it in goes back to standing there.
