arg.summary: 1 to leave it where it is, 0 to put it back

request.name: set_pointer

description.summary: how the pointing devices behave

request.description:
Sets the four things a session decides about a mouse: how fast the pointer travels for a given movement of the hand, how large the compositor draws it, how far one notch of a wheel carries the content under it, and which way that content goes.
The compositor's because every one of them is: three are libinput settings on a device the shell never opens — only the compositor holds the seat — and the fourth is the size of a picture the compositor is the one drawing. A shell could not carry any of them out.
**Every pointing device the seat has**, and not only the ones that are mice: a trackball, a touchpad and a controller's trackpad all move the same pointer, and a session where the speed applied to one of them and not the other would be a setting that works on some desks and not others. A device libinput says cannot do one of these keeps whatever it does — a mouse has no tap-to-click and a trackball may have no acceleration curve — and that is not an error.
Applied at once, and to the devices already plugged in as well as to the next one: this arrives while somebody is looking at the page they set it on, and a speed that waited for a replug would read as a press that did nothing.
speed is libinput's own acceleration setting in hundredths, -100 to 100, where 0 is the flat default every desktop starts at. It is not a multiplier and the scale is not linear — what libinput does with it depends on the device's own resolution — which is exactly why it is passed through rather than translated: the number the user chose on a bar means what libinput means by it, and the two cannot drift apart. Out of range is clamped rather than refused.
size is the cursor's nominal size in logical pixels, as XCURSOR_SIZE counts it. An XCursor theme carries a handful of drawn sizes and the nearest is used, so this is what the compositor asks for rather than what it necessarily gets. It changes the cursor this compositor draws — for the desktop itself and for every client that names a shape through cursor-shape-v1 — and it cannot change one an application draws for itself out of its own theme: a client reads XCURSOR_SIZE when it starts and this cannot reach back into one that is already running. A later client gets the new size, because the compositor exports it.
scroll is in per cent, 100 being one to one — the movement libinput reports, unchanged. libinput has no scroll speed of its own, so this is the compositor's own multiplication over the deltas it forwards, and it is applied to the discrete notch count as well as to the continuous value: a client that counts wheel detents must see the same setting a client that reads pixels sees, or the two disagree about how far one notch went.
natural is 1 for content that follows the fingers — the direction a touchscreen moves, and the direction a page moves under a hand on a touchpad — and 0 for the wheel's traditional direction. libinput's natural-scroll, passed through.
The four arrive together because they are one page, and because three of them are applied by walking the same device list: sending them separately would walk it four times for one press.
Not remembered by the compositor. The shell says what these are as soon as it connects — the same bargain set_application_scale is under, and for the same reason: the preference belongs to the page it was set on.

arg.name: speed
arg.summary: libinput acceleration in hundredths, -100 to 100; 0 is the default

arg.name: size
arg.summary: cursor size in logical pixels

arg.name: scroll
arg.summary: per cent of the movement reported; 100 is one to one

arg.name: natural
arg.summary: 1 for content that follows the fingers, 0 for the wheel's direction

request.name: set_keyboard_layout

description.summary: which arrangement every keyboard is set to

request.description:
Sets the xkb layout and variant the seat's keyboards use. The two names xkbcommon takes, unchanged: "pl" and "" for the Polish layout, "us" and "dvorak" for that arrangement of the American one.
The compositor's because the seat is. A shell has never held a keyboard — the one it draws types through zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1 with a keymap of its own — so nothing but the compositor can change what the keys on the desk produce.
Applied to the seat rather than per device, which is what xkb is: a keymap belongs to the seat's keyboard and every physical board on it types through the same one. It takes effect at once, including for clients already running: a Wayland client is sent the new keymap and the modifier state that goes with it.
A layout xkbcommon cannot compile is refused and the seat is left as it was. This is the one setting where falling back to something else would be worse than doing nothing: a machine whose keyboard silently became American is a machine somebody may not be able to type their password into. The compositor is expected to say so in its log and go on.
Not remembered by the compositor, on the same terms as set_application_scale and set_pointer: the preference belongs to the page it was set on. What the compositor's own configuration says is what it starts at, and this replaces it for the session.

arg.name: layout
arg.summary: xkb layout name, e.g. pl

arg.name: variant
arg.summary: xkb variant name, empty for the layout's own arrangement

request.name: set_menu_surface

description.summary: which surface of the shell's is its context menu

request.description:
Names a surface the shell draws its context menu on, and nothing else. A compositor draws that surface **in front of** the windows set_picture_in_picture floats, where it draws every other surface the shell owns behind them, and lets a press inside its input region be the shell's rather than the window's.
A floating window is drawn over everything, which is what the feature is — and a window the user has made large enough covers the very menu that offers to make it small again. On a console that is a dead end: there is no pointer to find an unseen row with, so a menu that cannot be seen cannot be answered. So one surface is allowed over such a window, and it is the one the menu is on.
A surface of its own rather than a rectangle of the shell's main one, because a menu's panel is **rounded** and a rectangle is not: a compositor lifting the panel's bounding box would put four square corners of the start screen over the video, where the video is what should be showing. Given its own surface the panel is exactly its own shape, whatever that shape is, and everything around it is transparent.
The shell is expected to make this a subsurface of the surface it would otherwise have drawn the menu on, so that the two commit together and no frame can show one without the other. A compositor draws it wherever the surface's own geometry puts it, which for a subsurface is where its parent and its offset put it; nothing here moves it.
Sent for as long as a menu is up and not a moment longer: before the frame that draws the first panel, and null again after the last one. Everything a compositor does about this is per-frame and per-press work, and none of it is owed on a session where nobody has opened a menu.
One at a time. A shell that draws menus on several surfaces names whichever is carrying the menu now; naming a second forgets the first. A null surface forgets whatever was named, and a surface that is destroyed is forgotten with it.

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: the shell's menu surface, or null to forget the last one

event.name: guide

description.summary: the guide binding was activated

event.description:
Sent when the user pressed the compositor's guide binding. The shell is expected to show or hide its overlay.
The compositor routes this itself because the shell has no keyboard focus while an application is running, which is precisely when the user needs a way back out of it.

event.name: keyboard

description.summary: the on-screen keyboard binding was activated

event.description:
Sent when the user pressed the compositor's on-screen keyboard binding. The shell is expected to show or hide its keyboard.
Routed by the compositor for the same reason the guide event is: the shell has no keyboard focus while an application is running, and a keyboard that could only be summoned by a client already holding the keys would be of no use to anyone.
Nothing else about typing goes over this interface. An application announces its text fields with zwp_text_input_v3, the shell hears about them as zwp_input_method_v2, and it types with zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1 — all three of which are standard, and none of which can express a binding the compositor has to intercept.

enum.name: volume_change

description.summary: what a volume key asked for

enum.description:
One step of the machine's own volume, in the direction the key pressed is printed with, or the switch that silences it.
A step rather than a value: which value one press is worth is a question about the control the shell draws, and the compositor has no opinion about it.

entry.name: up
entry.summary: one step louder

entry.name: down
entry.summary: one step quieter

entry.name: mute
entry.summary: silence it, or bring it back

event.name: volume

description.summary: a volume key was pressed

event.description:
Sent when the user pressed one of the keys the session's volume is set with. The shell is expected to move its own volume control by one step, or to silence the session, and to say on screen that it did.
Routed by the compositor for the reason the guide, keyboard and screenshot events are: a fullscreen application holds the keyboard, and a volume key that only worked while the shell had focus would be one that never worked over the game somebody was turning down.
The compositor forwards the press rather than setting the volume itself because the mixer belongs to the shell's half of the session. It is the shell that found out which sound server this machine has, that knows where the control stands, and that has somewhere to draw it; a compositor that shelled out to a mixer of its own would be a second opinion about the volume, one step out of step with the bar the user can see.
A key held down repeats, at the seat's own repeat rate, in the direction it was pressed. Mute does not: a switch held down is a switch thrown once.

arg.name: change
arg.summary: what the key asked for

event.name: output_pressed

description.summary: the user pressed an application on one display

event.description:
Sent when a pointer button or a finger landed on an application window, naming the display it landed on. The shell is expected to treat that display as the one the user is now driving, exactly as it does a press made on its own surface there.
A shell drawing itself on every display keeps its own idea of which one is being driven, and it can see a press move that for itself only while its own surfaces are in front — the press is delivered to the surface it was made on. Once an application is in front of it, it sees nothing at all: its overlay hands the clicks through so the application under it stays usable with a mouse, and so the very press that says "the user is over here now" is the one press the shell never hears about. On a machine with the launcher on one screen and a game on another, clicking the game left the launcher driving the first screen, which is where the guide then opened and where the next application started.
Only presses the shell has no other way to learn about are sent. A press on one of its own surfaces is delivered to that surface and is not repeated here — a shell that were told twice would move control on the compositor's word before it had read the press itself, turning a click that should only have claimed the display into one that also pressed whatever it landed on.
Nor is a press repeated on the display it was last sent for, so that clicking about inside a game does not wake the shell once per click. The compositor forgets that display whenever the shell names one with set_launch_output, because a shell that has moved on its own has to be able to hear about a press back on the display it left.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display the press landed on

event.name: typed

description.summary: the user pressed a key on a keyboard

event.description:
Sent when a key goes down on a keyboard the compositor can see: the user saying with their hands that the controller is not what they are holding. A shell is expected to put away what it is offering that controller — the corner chip naming the buttons that summon its on-screen keyboard, and the keyboard it would raise over a text field of its own accord.
Forwarded for the reason the guide, keyboard and volume events are, and with more at stake than any of them: while a fullscreen application owns the keyboard the shell is sent no keys whatsoever, and that is exactly the moment this answers for — somebody typing into a game's chat box, with a chip in the corner of the screen telling them which buttons to press for a keyboard they already have under their hands.
Only keys from a device the compositor reads itself. What a shell sends through zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1, and the arrows it sends with keyboard_key, are the shell typing on the user's behalf and are never reported back to it as the user typing.
Sent once, and then held back until the shell says the controller has been picked back up with controller_used. Somebody writing a message in a game would otherwise wake the shell once per letter to tell it something it was told at the first one. It is armed again whenever a shell binds this interface, because a shell that has just started has been told nothing.

event.name: foreground

description.summary: the foreground application changed

event.description:
Names the topmost application window so the shell can label its overlay. The title is empty when no application window exists, which is how the shell learns that an application it started has exited.
Sent once when the object is bound, and again on every change.
Describes the session as a whole, which is only the right answer for a shell that has one place to show it. Superseded by output_foreground, and not sent at all to clients bound at version 3 or above.

arg.name: title
arg.summary: window title, or empty when nothing is running

event.name: output_foreground

description.summary: the foreground application on one display changed

event.description:
Names the topmost application window on one display, or the empty string when that display has none.
A shell drawing a bar on every display needs this rather than the unqualified foreground event: its overlay belongs to the display the user is on, so labelling it with the session's topmost window offers to resume, or close, an application on a screen the user is not looking at.
Sent once per display when the object is bound, and again on every change.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: title
arg.summary: window title, or empty when nothing is running there

event.name: output_window

description.summary: one window on a display

event.description:
Describes one application window, for the shell's overview. A batch of these followed by output_windows_done replaces everything previously known about that display; windows are listed topmost first, so the first one is the application the user was just looking at.
The size is what the window occupies on the display, which is not always the logical size its client was configured at: an application drawing larger than life is configured smaller than the screen by that factor and then drawn back out across the whole of it. The shell is given the size on the screen because that is what both of its questions are about — aspect-fitting a selection frame to the card the compositor will draw, and deciding whether an application covers the bar, which is what stops the shell drawing a start screen nobody can see. Told the configured size instead, a session with larger applications never believed any of them covered anything.
Sent once per display when a version 4 object is bound, and again whenever the display's windows or their titles change.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: id
arg.summary: stable handle for activate_window

arg.name: title
arg.summary: window title

arg.name: width
arg.summary: logical width

arg.name: height
arg.summary: logical height

event.name: output_window_app_id

description.summary: what one listed window's application is

event.description:
Names the application one window of the batch belongs to, the way the application names itself — its xdg_toplevel app_id, or an X11 window's class. Sent immediately after the output_window it describes, and only when there is one to send: a client that set neither leaves its window with no name rather than an empty one.
output_window carries the *title*, which is what a card prints and exactly what nothing can be matched on: a title is a document, a directory, a track that is playing. A shell that has to answer "is this application already running?" — as it must before starting a second copy of something the user only wanted to come back to — needs the name that stays the same while the application runs, and that it can also work out from the application's desktop entry before it has ever been started.
Carried per window rather than per display, unlike output_app_id, because the question is about every window on the display and not only the one in front.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: id
arg.summary: the window, from the preceding output_window

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: the application's own name for itself

event.name: output_window_pid

description.summary: which process drew one listed window

event.description:
Names the process behind one window of the batch: the pid of the client that created it, or for an X11 window the pid the window itself advertises. Sent immediately after the output_window it describes, and only when the compositor knows one — a client that connected over a socket carrying no credentials, or an X11 window whose owner set no _NET_WM_PID, leaves its window without this rather than with a zero.
It exists because a window says nothing about who started it. The class an application announces is a name somebody chose for a program, and a great many programs are started by something other than the user: a game is started by a store client, a document by a file manager, a window by whatever was already running. A shell that has to answer "which of the things I started did this window turn out to be" can otherwise only answer it by timing — the window that appeared while I was waiting — which is right until two things appear at once.
The pid is a handle onto the process table and nothing more. What can be read from it is the same thing anything else on the session could read: this compositor grants no access with it and makes no claim about what the process is.

arg.summary: the display

event.name: output_windows_done

description.summary: the window list for a display is complete

event.description: Ends a batch of output_window events. The batch is the whole truth for that display: a done event immediately after the last batch's windows with none in between means the display has no windows at all.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

event.name: unseen_window

description.summary: one window that is being kept off the screen

event.description:
Describes one window the compositor is hiding on the shell's own instructions — see keep_out_of_sight. A batch of these followed by unseen_windows_done replaces everything previously known about them.
The counterpart of output_window, and deliberately not part of it: a hidden window is not on a display as far as anything else is concerned, so it is not listed with one, is not drawn a card, and is not something to switch to. It is listed at all so that the shell can see what its own instruction is covering, and let one window through where the application has stopped to ask something. See let_this_window_be_seen.
A window let through leaves this list, because it is no longer being kept off the screen: it appears in the display's ordinary window list instead. So the two lists together are still the whole truth, and a window that has gone from both has gone.
Sent once when a version 40 object is bound, and again whenever the hidden windows, their names or their titles change. A session with nothing hidden — which is nearly all of them — sends one empty batch and never speaks of it again.

arg.summary: stable handle, named as output_window names one

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: the application's own name for itself

arg.name: title

event.name: unseen_windows_done

description.summary: the hidden window list is complete

event.description: Ends a batch of unseen_window events. The batch is the whole truth: a done event with no windows before it means nothing is being kept off the screen.

event.name: output_app_id

description.summary: what the foreground application on one display is

event.description:
Names the topmost application window on one display the way the application itself is named — its xdg_toplevel app_id, or an X11 window's class — or the empty string when that display has none.
output_foreground carries the window *title*, which is what a menu should print and exactly what a setting must not be filed under: a title is a document name, a working directory, a track that is playing. A shell remembering a choice per application needs the name that does not change while the application runs, and is the same the next time it is started.
Sent alongside output_foreground: once per display when the object is bound, and again on every change.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: application identity, or empty when nothing is running there

event.name: output_hdr

description.summary: what one display can do in HDR, and what it is doing

event.description:
Says whether a display can be driven in high dynamic range, and whether it currently is.
A shell offering the setting has to be able to answer "why is this doing nothing" before the user asks it, and there are three separate reasons it might: the display never claimed HDR in its EDID, the driver has no colour pipeline to do the encoding with, or the session is running nested inside another compositor and owns no connector at all. All three come back as supported = 0, because the shell's answer is the same in each case and the reason is in the compositor's log.
enabled is what the compositor is actually doing, not what it was last asked for. They differ exactly when a request could not be carried out, which is the case the shell must not present as success.
max_luminance is the peak the display reports in its EDID, which is what a shell should show as its "display default" peak brightness. 0 when the display does not say — an HDR display is not obliged to, and one that stays quiet is not saying zero.
Sent once per display when a version 9 object is bound, and again whenever any of it changes.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: supported
arg.summary: 1 when this display can be driven in HDR

arg.name: enabled
arg.summary: 1 when it currently is

arg.name: max_luminance
arg.summary: the display's own peak luminance in cd/m², 0 when it does not say

enum.name: hdr_control

description.summary: which HDR settings a display can actually honour

enum.description: A display being drivable in HDR does not mean every control does something on it. The colour pipeline a driver exposes decides that, and what it exposes varies by hardware generation on the same driver.

entry.name: gamut
entry.summary: sRGB colour intensity does something on this display

entry.name: gamut_exact
entry.summary: and the conversion it does is the exact one

event.name: output_hdr_controls

description.summary: which HDR settings do something on one display

event.description:
Says which of the HDR settings this display can honour, as a bitmask of hdr_control.
A shell has to be able to tell a control that is off from a control that does nothing, and a control that does the thing exactly from one that does it approximately. sRGB colour intensity is the case this exists for, and it has all three answers.
It is implemented as the CRTC's colour matrix. Where the CRTC has no matrix at all, gamut is unset: there is nowhere to put the conversion, the picture's primaries are sent as BT.2020's, and a page that went on offering the choice would be describing a display that does not exist.
Where there is a matrix but no degamma stage in front of it, gamut is set and gamut_exact is not. A matrix is a gamut rotation when it acts on linear light; acting on sRGB-coded values it leaves white, black and the whole grey axis untouched — every row of it sums to 1 — and brings saturated colour close rather than exactly right. The setting works at every position; it is simply not the same picture a display engine with a degamma stage would show, and a shell is expected to say so rather than imply an accuracy that is not there.
Where both are set, the conversion is the exact one.
This is a separate event from output_hdr rather than another argument on it because an event's arguments cannot change once it has shipped.
A shell bound below version 42 is told only gamut, and should read it the way it always did: as the exact conversion, which is what every display it was told about could do.
Sent alongside output_hdr: once per display when a version 10 object is bound, and again whenever it changes.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: controls
arg.summary: the settings this display can honour

event.name: output_night_light

description.summary: whether one display can be warmed, and whether it is

event.description:
Says whether a display's picture can be tinted towards a warmer colour temperature, and whether it currently is.
supported is 1 when this display has a gamma ramp the compositor can commit to. It is a much lower bar than HDR — no EDID claim is needed and nothing is asked of the link — so almost every real connector clears it. What does not is a session running nested inside another compositor, which owns no CRTC and therefore no ramp; there the setting can be remembered but never carried out, and a page that went on offering it would be describing a display that does not exist.
active is what the compositor is actually doing, not what it was last asked for. The two differ exactly when a request could not be carried out, which is the case a shell must not present as success.
Nothing here says *why* the light is on: whether that is a schedule or a switch is the shell's own business, since the schedule never left it. See set_output_night_light.
Sent once per display when a version 20 object is bound, and again whenever either value changes.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display

arg.name: supported
arg.summary: 1 when this display's picture can be warmed

arg.name: active
arg.summary: 1 when it currently is

event.name: output_place

description.summary: where one display stands in the layout

event.description:
Says which place a display holds in the row the compositor lays its displays out in — 0 is the first one, which on a left-to-right layout is the leftmost screen — and, by being sent at all, that this display's place is the shell's to set.
The places reported are always 0 to n-1 over the displays reported, with no gaps: they are positions in one list, not identities. A display this compositor does not place is left out of that list entirely rather than given a place it does not have — one pinned to a position by the compositor's own config, which takes no part in the arrangement, and every display on a session that mirrors them onto the same region, where there is no order to be in. A shell listing what it is sent therefore offers the setting exactly where it does something.
place is where the display actually is, not what was last asked for. The two differ when a request could not be carried out, which is the case a shell must not present as success.
Every display whose place changed is sent one, so a trade between two of them arrives as two events. Sent once per display when a version 21 object is bound, and again whenever the arrangement changes — including when a display is plugged in or unplugged, which renumbers the ones that outlast it.

event.name: output_mode

description.summary: one mode a display can be driven at

event.description:
Describes one entry of a display's mode list. A batch of these ending in output_modes_done replaces everything previously known about that display, the way the overview's window list does.
The list is the connector's own, so it says what the hardware will actually take rather than what a client would like. A backend with no connectors — a nested session, whose size is its window's — reports no modes at all, which is the truthful answer to "what else could this be driven at" and not the same as reporting the one it is at.

Sizes are the mode's own pixels, before scale and transform. Two entries may share a size and differ only in refresh; both are real choices, and a shell listing them should say which is which.
Sent once per display when a version 11 object is bound, and again whenever the list or the current mode changes — including after a set_output_mode, which is how a shell learns whether the change it asked for happened.

description.summary: what came of a capture_window request

Answers exactly one capture_window request, whether or not it worked.

It is empty when nothing was written — the window had gone, it had no pixels to read, or the file could not be created — and the reason is in the compositor's log. A shell showing the user that a screenshot was taken should show it when this arrives and not when it asked, because until then it does not know.

description.summary: how one display's picture is turned

Says how a display's picture is currently turned, and by being sent at all, that this display's orientation is the shell's to set.
wl_output.geometry carries a transform too, and it is not the same statement. That one describes what a client should do about the output it is drawing on, and a compositor may advertise it for a display whose orientation it does not own — a nested session, whose window is turned by the compositor above it, or a backend whose output carries a transform of its own to compensate for how it draws. This event is sent only for displays this compositor turns itself, so a shell listing them offers the setting exactly where it does something.
transform is what the compositor is actually drawing at, not what it was last asked for. They differ when a request could not be carried out, which is the case a shell must not present as success.
Sent once per display when a version 16 object is bound, and again whenever it changes.

event.name: screenshot

description.summary: the screenshot binding was activated

event.description:
Sent when the user pressed the compositor's screenshot binding, naming the display they were on. The shell is expected to answer with a capture_output request for that display.
Routed by the compositor for the reason the guide and keyboard events are: a fullscreen application holds the keyboard, and a screenshot key that only worked while the shell had focus would be one that never worked over the game somebody wanted a picture of.
The compositor asks rather than simply taking the picture itself because the two halves of a screenshot live in different processes. Only the compositor has the pixels, and only the shell knows where a user's pictures go — which folder the desktop records for them, in the language the account was made in, and what the file should be called. So the binding comes here and the path goes back.
The display named is the one the user is driving, which is where the keyboard that pressed the binding is. A shell may photograph a different one, or every one; nothing here obliges it to take the picture at all.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the display the binding was pressed on

event.name: share_request

event.description:

event.name: screen_is_black

description.summary: the curtain is down on every display

event.description:
Answers cover_in_black: every display the compositor is driving has put a frame on screen with the black fully drawn over it.
It is sent once per curtain, and only on the way down. A client asking for the black because it is about to end the session waits for this before it does — that is the whole point of the request, and it is the one moment at which nothing that happens next can be seen.
A display the compositor cannot draw on — one that is off, or has been unplugged — takes no part: it is showing nothing already. With no display left at all the event follows the fade immediately, because a session with nothing to black out has nothing to wait for.

event.name: output_in_use

description.summary: an application is in front of this display

event.description:
Whether what is in front of this display is an application — anything the user opened, whatever started it — rather than the shell being the whole of what is on the screen. A display showing nothing but the start screen is 0. A game, a film, a browser, an emulator and Valve's own storefront are all 1: the shell has no business ranking what somebody chose to open, and every one of them is a picture somebody is looking at.
Whether there is such a window there at all is a question only this side can answer. The shell is told what the window in front of each display calls itself, and that is exactly what cannot be relied on: an application reaches the screen as steam_app_..., as its own name, or as nothing at all, and an empty name is both "no window" and "a window that never said".
Sent when the answer changes, per display, and on binding. A shell that never asks about it can ignore it entirely; what it is for is the rule that rests the *other* screens while somebody is using one of them.

event.name: output_drawing

description.summary: something on this display is still painting

event.description:
Whether any application on this display has put a new frame up recently. A film playing on the second screen keeps this at 1; the same film paused, a page nobody is scrolling, and a display with no application on it at all are all 0.
The shell cannot answer this for itself. It is told which windows are on which display, and it is told what they are called, but a window that has stopped drawing looks exactly like one that has not from the other side of the compositor — the frames go from the client to us.
It is what tells a screen that can be rested from one that is being watched. A still picture is the thing an OLED panel is damaged by and the thing nobody minds losing; a moving one is neither.
Recently means the last few seconds, which is deliberately long enough that a film dropping frames is still drawing and short enough that a paused one has stopped. Sent when the answer changes, per display, and on binding.

event.name: output_pointer

description.summary: the pointer is moving over this display

event.description:
Sent while the pointer is being moved, naming the display it is over.
The shell sees the pointer only where its own surfaces are in front, and that is precisely not where this matters: over an application, and over a display whose picture the shell has asked to have taken away, the movement is delivered somewhere else or to nobody. So the compositor names the display, exactly as output_pressed names the one a press landed on.
Throttled rather than streamed: it is sent the moment the pointer arrives on a different display, and after that at most once every two seconds for as long as it goes on moving. A pointer standing still sends nothing at all. That is enough for a shell timing out a display it has left alone, and it is a long way short of a motion event.

event.name: pip_menu

description.summary: the user asked for the floating window's menu

event.description:
Sent when the user presses the right button on the floating window a set_picture_in_picture is about. The shell is expected to raise its context menu over that rectangle and to send back whatever is chosen — pip_menu_command for the rows only a compositor can carry out, and move_window_to_output for the two that move the window between displays, which is what that request already means for every other window.
The compositor routes this itself for the same reason it routes the guide binding: the shell has no pointer focus over an application, and this window is drawn in front of one. It is not offered a press it cannot see.
The rectangle is the whole window as the user sees it — the surround included, since that is what the pointer is over — in the display's own logical coordinates, so a shell can hand it straight to whatever it grows a menu out of.
A shell that answers nothing has answered "cancel", which is what the row of that name does: nothing is held open on this side while the menu is up, and the press has already been withheld from the window's own client.

Describes one window a set_picture_in_picture is floating, so that a shell with no pointer can offer the user something to do to it. Windows are listed topmost first, and the batch ends with pip_windows_done.

What this is for is the window itself — where it is, so a menu can be grown out of it and the user can be shown which of two videos they are about to move.
The rectangle is the whole window as the user sees it, surround included, in the display's own logical coordinates: the same rectangle pip_menu carries, and for the same reason.

request.name: ask_for_the_picture_behind

description.summary: hand over a buffer for what is drawn behind the shell

request.description:
Asks the compositor to draw, into `buffer`, what it is compositing on this display behind the shell's own surfaces — and to say when it has.
The shell draws glass, and glass shows what is behind it. Everything the shell itself draws it can read back from its own frame, and the wallpaper it can evaluate, because it is the same function that paints it. What it can neither read nor evaluate is another client: a game, or the video in a floating window. Without this a pane standing over one of those reproduces the wallpaper instead — a picture that is not there.
`layer` says which side of the shell's own surfaces to draw. `below` is everything between the wallpaper and the surface the shell draws its session on: the application windows. `above` is everything the compositor draws in *front* of that surface and behind the context menu: the windows set_picture_in_picture floats. The two are separate because the shell has to put its own frame between them, and it draws that at full resolution.
The picture is the compositor's own elements, scaled down to the size of the buffer, on transparent: a pane composites it over the wallpaper it evaluates itself, so what nothing covers must arrive covering nothing. Small is expected and is the point — a pane frosts what it transmits, so what it wants is a blurred picture, and a small one read back per frame is cheaper than a large one. The compositor scales to whatever size the buffer is.
One buffer is one picture. The compositor fills it, sends the_picture_behind, and then leaves it alone until it is handed another — so a shell that stops asking stops being charged for the readback, and a shell that wants one per frame asks once per frame. Nothing is drawn for a display no buffer is pending on.
The buffer must be wl_shm, ABGR8888 or XBGR8888 — the order a renderer reads a picture back in, so that a copy is all there is between the two. A buffer of a size the compositor cannot use is answered with the_picture_behind carrying a width and height of zero rather than an error: a picture is an improvement to a pane, never a reason to end a session over.

request.name: set_window_floating

description.summary: make a window float in a corner, or stop it floating

request.description:
Says of one window what set_picture_in_picture says of the session: that it floats. It is the same answer the window's title gives by itself — see set_picture_in_picture, which is where what floating *is* is written down — taken out of the compositor's hands for this one window and given to the user.
Both directions, because they are one sentence. A video in a corner that the user wants to watch properly is told zero: it stops floating, and is laid out, listed, focused and closed exactly as every other window on the session is — which on this shell means filling the display it is on. An application the user wants out of the way while they do something else is told one: it is taken out of that layout and given the corner, the size and the surround a browser's picture-in-picture window gets, whatever it calls itself. A second request naming only one of the two would be one place for the other to be got wrong.
What is said here outranks the title from then on, and outlasts the window ceasing to be called Picture-in-Picture: the user has said what they want this window to be, and a browser retitling it is not them changing their mind. It is remembered against the window and dies with it.
Refused, with nothing done, while set_picture_in_picture has the feature switched off: a session that does not want floating windows must not be given one from a menu, and one put in a corner there would be a window with no corner to be got out of.
Also refused for a window whose geometry is its client's own business — an X11 menu, notification, splash or override-redirect window — which is the one kind that can never be given a corner. Silently, as a request naming a window that is gone is: a menu row is a thing the user pressed, not a protocol error.
How the change is drawn is the compositor's. This one grows the window out of its corner to fill the display, the same flight a window makes when it is restored from a tile, and lets one arriving in a corner arrive the way any floating window does.

request.name: offer_kind

description.summary: one kind of file the question coming next will accept

request.description:
Names one pattern of one kind, for the ask_to_pick_files that follows it. Sent as many times as there are patterns, which is how an application that accepts "Images" made of *.png, *.jpg and *.webp says so.
Patterns sharing a name are one kind. The order is the order the application gave, and the first kind named is the one the question opens on, exactly as it is in every other desktop's chooser — an application that put "Images" first meant the user to see images.
It carries the same id as the ask_to_pick_files it belongs to, and it must come before it: a kind offered afterwards has arrived after the question was put on screen and is ignored. Nothing accumulates in the compositor — each of these is carried straight to the shell as a pick_kind event, in the order it was sent, and it is the shell that gathers them against the question they name.
Offering no kind at all is an application that will take any file, which is the common case and is not a mistake.

request.name: ask_to_pick_files

description.summary: ask the user to choose a file, some files, or a folder

request.description:
Puts a file question to the session shell: this application wants a file chosen, and here is what it will take. The answer comes back as pick_answered, always, so a portal waiting on it is never left waiting.
Sent by the session's desktop portal for the same reason ask_to_share is and along the same road, and it is worth reading that request first: the portal cannot draw, only the shell can, and only the compositor can reach the shell while a fullscreen application holds the screen.
id is the asking client's own number for this question, unique among the questions it currently has outstanding, and is quoted back in the answer. app_id is what the application asking calls itself, for the shell to name in the question; it may be empty, and a shell should then say so rather than showing an empty name.
title is what the application called the question — "Open Image", "Select a folder" — and may be empty, in which case the shell says what the purpose is in its own words. accept is the word the application wants on the row that answers, and may likewise be empty. Neither is trusted for anything but its own line of text.
name is what a new file is called to begin with, and means nothing for any purpose but a_new_file. at is an absolute path the question should open in, and may be empty; a shell may ignore it, and must ignore one that is not a directory it can list — an application does not get to decide what the user is looking at.
The question goes to every other client bound to this interface, and never back to the one that asked, on exactly the terms ask_to_share's does. Refused outright when nobody can be asked, for the same reason: a file handed over without anybody being asked is the thing this request exists to prevent.

event.name: switch_window

description.summary: the user is walking the session's applications

event.description:
Sent when the user pressed the compositor's switch binding — Alt+Tab, and Alt+Shift+Tab the other way — with the modifier still held down. The shell is expected to show its overlay with the window deck in front, and to step the highlight one card in the direction given.
Routed by the compositor for the reason the guide, keyboard and volume events are, and here it is not merely that the application holds the keyboard: the application holding it is the one being switched away from. A switcher that only worked while the shell had focus would be a switcher for a session with nothing to switch between.
One event per press. The compositor does not repeat a held binding, so a thumb left on Tab steps one card rather than thirty.
Nothing is switched by this. It says where the user has got to; what they land on is taken when switch_done arrives.

Sent once when the shell binds, and again whenever the seat's keymap is changed by anything — including by the shell's own set_keyboard_layout, so that a request the compositor refused is not left showing as though it had been carried out.
This exists because the shell cannot find the answer out. What a session starts at is the compositor's own configuration file, which no other process in the session has opened, and a settings page that could not say what was in force would have nothing to mark on the first machine it was ever opened on.
The two names are xkbcommon's, as set_keyboard_layout takes them. variant is empty for a layout's own arrangement.

event.name: switch_done

description.summary: the modifier the walk was held under came up

event.description:
Sent when the user let go of the modifier. The shell is expected to take whatever its highlight is on — that application coming back to the front and taking the keyboard with it — and to put its overlay away.
Never sent without a switch_window before it: a modifier let go of by somebody who never asked for the deck is not an answer to anything.
Nor is it sent where the walk was interrupted rather than finished — the session losing the keyboard to another virtual terminal. Those keys came up on the compositor's word rather than under the user's hand, and a shell that took a card on them would be switching applications behind somebody's back. The overlay is left standing instead, where every other way of driving it still reaches it.
